decisions.title: Separate Stable Policy from Runtime Fragments
decisions.description: The system prompt is split into two categories: stable policy (role definition, safety rules, non-negotiable constraints) and runtime fragments (working directory, available tools, memory context, task state). Stable policy rarely changes and benefits from prompt caching. Runtime fragments change frequently. Keeping them separate means the model always sees the same foundation, and only the dynamic parts vary.
decisions.alternatives: One monolithic prompt string is simpler but grows uncontrollably and defeats prompt caching. Generating the entire prompt from templates every time works but loses the stability that helps the model anchor its behavior.

decisions.title: Prompt Sections Assembled in a Defined Order
decisions.description: The prompt builder assembles sections in a fixed order: stable policy, runtime state, tool definitions, memory injection, task state, and recovery hints. This ordering matters because the model processes earlier sections first and may weight them more heavily. Safety rules before tool definitions means the model sees constraints before capabilities.
decisions.alternatives: Alphabetical or insertion-order assembly is simpler but produces unpredictable behavior. Allowing each section to specify its own priority leads to conflicts. A fixed pipeline is explicit and debuggable.

decisions.title: The Prompt Pipeline IS the Control Plane
decisions.description: What the model sees determines how it behaves. The prompt assembly pipeline controls which information is available, in what order, and with what emphasis. This makes the prompt builder the agent's true control plane -- not the tool dispatch, not the permission system, but the input construction pipeline. Understanding this framing is crucial: changing the prompt changes the agent's behavior more directly than changing any other component.
decisions.alternatives: Treating the system prompt as a static configuration file misses the opportunity to dynamically control behavior. Treating it as a free-form string template loses the structure that makes predictable assembly possible.
